title: How Schools Can Counter “The End of Reading”
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler responds to Rose Horowitch's viral Atlantic cover story arguing that America is entering a 'postliterate' society where people read constantly but only in snippets. Wexler contextualizes the reading crisis: Americans can read, but the sustained, complex reading that builds analytical thinking has been displaced by social media and short-form content. Schools exacerbated the decline by focusing on reading comprehension 'skills' and mimicking standardized test formats with short excerpts, while schools serving low-income students assigned even fewer full books. Wexler argues that the situation is less bleak than Horowitch suggests, pointing to literacy curricula incorporating whole books and knowledge-building gaining ground at the elementary level. She notes that writing instruction is probably the most effective way to build analytical and complex thinking, a practice underemphasized in current schooling. A functioning democracy depends on the cognitive capacities of the electorate, and a postliterate society, where misinformation spreads instantly, may be more dangerous than an illiterate one—making school-based interventions urgent.
points: Americans are reading more than ever but overwhelmingly in snippets—emails, texts, social posts—while the sustained, deep reading that builds logical and analytical thinking has sharply declined, especially among adolescents.

Schools worsened the crisis by adopting short-excerpt test formats and focusing on generic comprehension 'skills' over background knowledge; schools serving low-income students assigned the fewest full books, compounding educational inequity.

Evidence-informed literacy curricula incorporating whole books and knowledge-building are gaining traction at the elementary level, and writing instruction is identified as the most effective lever for building deep analytical thinking.
quotes: Americans can read, by and large, and in fact they’re probably reading more than ever. But what they’re reading are snippets: emails, texts, brief posts on social media.

That kind of reading, the evidence suggests, brings cognitive benefits: the ability to think logically, analytically, deeply, and perhaps creatively. By the same token, Horowitch argues, the disappearance of that kind of reading will lead to—has perhaps already led to—cognitive decline.

Those who absorb information through listening rather than reading respond best to epithets, repetition, and descriptions of violence, and they’re not bothered by self-contradiction because they can’t remember what the speaker said before.
Under pressure to raise standardized reading test scores, educators have mimicked the test format: short excerpts or brief passages followed by comprehension questions.
A functioning democracy depends on the cognitive abilities of the electorate. And a postliterate society could pose more of a threat than an illiterate one.
rather than a dirge of despair, we need a call to action—and that call should focus on schools, which are in a unique position to act.
